source: Barbieri et al. (2023) Meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance (poster, interim)
finding: Interim meta-analysis of worked examples vs no examples in math. Average effect is small to medium and varies a lot.
numbers: 40 articles, 49 studies, 185 effect sizes (46 experimental, 3 quasi-experimental). RVE g = 0.43, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.55. Effect sizes ranged -1.80 to 4.66; 41 negative, 144 positive. I2 = 94.46%. Meta-regression: no moderator significant (example type, format, grade, content).
limits: Interim poster; the published version changed the numbers. Search covered ERIC, PsycINFO, ProQuest theses. Math only. Very high heterogeneity means the mean hides large spread.
agent_relevance: Expect a positive average gain but with big variation by setup. 41 of 185 contrasts went the wrong way, so test examples on our own tasks.

source: Barbieri et al. (2023) Meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance (published)
finding: Published version: 43 studies, medium effect g = 0.48, same for practice and first learning. Self-explanation prompts added on top of examples did not help.
numbers: 43 studies, g = 0.48 (RVE, p = 0.01). Both practice use and initial acquisition give medium effects. Self-explanation prompts moderated the effect negatively; correct-only examples beat incorrect-only or mixed sets.
quote: Correct examples are particularly beneficial for learning overall.
limits: Secondary summary (blog) of the paper; Springer full text was blocked, so moderator estimates are not read first-hand. Mostly grades 6-12 algebra and geometry. Poster reported no significant moderators, the final paper reports some.
agent_relevance: Library entries should be correct solved cases. Do not assume that adding explain-it-yourself prompts helps; it may hurt when explanations are weak.

source: Barbieri et al. (2023) published abstract via search summaries
finding: Abstract-level facts: 8,033 abstracts screened, causal studies with random assignment, g = 0.48.
numbers: 8,033 abstracts screened; g = 0.48, p = 0.01; robust variance estimation.
limits: Not opened: publisher page redirected to a login gate. Counted as unopened.
agent_relevance: Treat moderator details as unverified until the full text is read.

source: Sweller (2023) The development of cognitive load theory: replication crises and incorporation of other theories
finding: Sweller states the effect first failed to replicate outside algebra. Algebra worked examples (Sweller and Cooper 1985; Cooper and Sweller 1987) beat problem solving, but geometry and kinematics examples did not.
numbers: Algebra: multiple supporting experiments. Geometry and physics kinematics: no worked example effect, failures lasted several years. Cause found: split attention in the standard geometry layout. Physically integrating text and diagram restored the effect (Tarmizi and Sweller 1988; Ward and Sweller 1990).
quote: we had our own, very strong examples of multiple, replication failures.
limits: Author account of his own programme, not an independent replication. No effect sizes given.
agent_relevance: An example that makes the reader hunt between parts can lose the benefit. Examples stored for our agent must have steps and referents in one place.

source: Sweller (2023) replication crises: expertise reversal as explanation of mixed results
finding: The worked example effect appears only for high element interactivity material. For low element interactivity material, problem solving is better (reverse effect).
numbers: Cites Chen et al. 2015, 2016a,b, 2017 and Kalyuga et al. 2001 for the reverse effect. No pooled numbers given.
quote: these are not replication failures, they are theory failures due to not recognising the critical variable of element interactivity.
limits: Explains away mixed results after the fact; the claim is only as good as the independent estimates of element interactivity and expertise. Hard to falsify.
agent_relevance: Use examples when a step has many interacting parts for this agent; skip them on easy, low-interaction steps.

source: Sweller (2023) worked example effect versus discovery and problem-based learning
finding: Sweller says randomised trials of worked examples with school problems frequently found novices learn more from studying than solving, the reverse of what discovery learning predicts.
numbers: Cites Sweller and Cooper 1985, Cooper and Sweller 1987, Paas 1992, Paas and van Merrienboer 1994. No sample sizes given in this text.
quote: worked examples frequently proved superior to actually solving the equivalent problems
limits: Word 'frequently' means not always. Narrative review by the theory's author.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the agent solved cases before asking it to search for solutions on new problem types.

source: Sweller (2011) Cognitive load theory chapter: worked example effect, mechanism
finding: Mechanism: problem search involves many interacting elements and heavy extraneous load; a worked example only contains elements needed for the schema, so load falls.
numbers: Founding demonstration is Sweller and Cooper (1985), algebra such as (a+b)/c=d solve for a. Described as replicated on a large number of occasions; no counts given.
limits: Theory chapter, no data tables. The 'large number' of replications is the author's claim.
agent_relevance: Our subgoal library is the schema-store side of this; the agent should get solved subgoal chains, not just search.

source: Sweller (2011) chapter: ill-defined domains and expertise reversal
finding: Effect also shown for ill-defined material (Rourke and Sweller 2009, learning furniture designers' styles). With more expertise, the difference shrinks, then reverses.
numbers: Expertise reversal for worked examples shown by Kalyuga, Chandler, Tuovinen and Sweller (2001). Redundancy of the example for experts is the proposed cause.
limits: No effect sizes given. Cited studies not opened here.
agent_relevance: Open mode tasks may still gain from cases, but order matters: cases first, then fade.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Worked-example effect
finding: Encyclopedia summary lists boundary results: Ward and Sweller (1990) found examples can be no better or worse than problem solving under some conditions.
numbers: Quilici and Mayer (1996): three examples per problem type did not beat one on sorting problems by type. Paas (1992): completion problems (half worked) matched fully worked. Pillay (1994): three intermediate stages beat one, if gaps are small.
limits: Tertiary source; no effect sizes. Treat as a pointer list.
agent_relevance: More examples per type is not always better; completion tasks are a cheap middle step.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Worked-example effect: tutoring field studies
finding: Lists Schwonke et al. (2009): two experiments with Geometry Cognitive Tutor. Example-enhanced tutor needed less learning time; experiment 2 replicated the efficiency gain and found deeper conceptual understanding.
numbers: Van Gog, Kester and Paas (2011), circuit troubleshooting: example-only and example-problem pairs beat problem-example pairs and pure problem solving with less mental effort. Nievelstein et al. (2013), law cases: efficiency benefit for novice and advanced students.
limits: No numbers; secondary. Check originals before citing figures.
agent_relevance: Gain is mostly efficiency (same learning in less time), not a big accuracy jump. This fits a token-budget agent.

source: Salden, Aleven, Schwonke, Renkl (2009) Are worked examples and tutored problem solving synergistic? (ISLS proceedings)
finding: Three conditions in a geometry Cognitive Tutor: standard tutored problem solving, fixed fading of examples, adaptive fading. Adaptive fading gave highest delayed transfer.
numbers: Lab study (Freiburg, German high school, random assignment): adaptive fading higher on immediate and delayed post-test than both others. Classroom study (Pittsburgh vocational school, delayed test 3 weeks later): adaptive beat problem solving on delayed transfer only; the lab effect was not fully replicated. N and effect sizes not given in this short paper.
quote: Tutored problem solving and worked examples, adaptively faded, are synergistic, not redundant, forms of support.
limits: Short proceedings abstract; no N or effect sizes. Classroom effect weaker than lab. Fixed fading did not help in the classroom comparison.
agent_relevance: Fade by the learner's own performance, not by a fixed schedule. For the agent: show a solved subgoal, then withdraw steps once it passes a check.

source: Schwonke et al. (2007) fixed fading, as summarised in Salden et al. (2009)
finding: Earlier two studies found tutored example fading on a fixed schedule gave more transfer than tutored problem solving alone, and was less time consuming.
numbers: No numbers in the summary.
limits: Second-hand summary; fixed-fading advantage did not show in the later classroom comparison.
agent_relevance: Efficiency gain is the safer claim than a learning-outcome gain.

source: Chen et al. and Kalyuga et al., expertise reversal as moderator (via Sweller 2011 and 2023)
finding: Moderator of the effect is prior knowledge. Procedure A beats B for novices; the gap narrows with expertise, then B wins.
numbers: Reversal shown for worked examples, split-attention (Kalyuga, Chandler, Sweller 1998) and modality (2000) effects. No pooled sizes in the sources opened.
limits: Primary experiments not read. Link to sibling subfield 04 (expertise reversal).
agent_relevance: The agent should skip examples for subgoals it has already solved reliably in this session.

source: Procedural ABICAP (2025) agent-based model of procedural learning
finding: A simulated learner model reproduces the worked example effect and expertise reversal: passive study beats active and constructive early, then the order flips.
numbers: 20-node Watts-Strogatz knowledge graph, 50 simulated learners per condition, 60 steps, mastery threshold 0.8. Parameters: prior b=0.6; cognitive load passive 0.5, active 0.65, constructive 0.75, interactive 0.8. Passive at least as good as active and constructive until about step 35; after that active and constructive overtake.
limits: A model with hand-set parameters, not data from people or LLMs. Authors call the replication preliminary and say no specific study was matched.
agent_relevance: Supports a schedule: study solved cases early, shift to self-generated work after some mastery.

source: Hou et al. (2026) CoMeT: adaptive scaffolding AI tutor that escalates and fades
finding: LLM coding tutor raises help when the learner fails at a decision and fades it on take-up (adaptive fading idea). Within-subject test with 131 adults on three Python tasks.
numbers: N = 131 completed all three tasks (162 began). Three tutors: CoMeT, unrestricted assistant, question-only tutor. CoMeT matched question-only tutor on demand, delivered artifacts about twice as often, frustrated learners less than question-only tutor, delegation and load unchanged. Full answer surrendered in 1 of 16 sessions vs 1 of 6 for question-only tutor.
limits: Outcomes are behaviour and self-report, not learning gain or exam score. Adults, introductory Python, short sessions. Worked examples are a small part of the tutor.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a code-controlled escalate-and-fade rule works for an LLM-run helper. Not direct proof of a worked example effect for LLMs.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Towards understanding chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Model-side analogue of worked examples with errors: invalid reasoning in demonstrations still keeps most of the benefit; relevance and coherence matter more than validity.
numbers: text-davinci-002, GSM8K answer accuracy: standard 15.4, CoT 48.5, invalid reasoning 39.5, no coherence 23.1, no relevance 11.0. Bamboogle answer F1: CoT 45.2, invalid 39.4, no relevance 23.9. Intrinsic metrics: invalid reasoning kept over 90% of CoT.
limits: Prompted LLMs only; four models, two main benchmarks. Accuracy fell about 9 points on GSM8K with invalid steps, so invalid is not free.
agent_relevance: A wrong solved example costs less than an irrelevant one. Check that library cases match the query's objects and steps first, correctness second.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the role of demonstrations
finding: Replacing gold labels in demonstrations with random labels barely hurt in-context learning on classification and multiple-choice tasks, across 12 models including GPT-3.
numbers: k = 16 demonstrations, 5 seeds; macro-F1 and accuracy with random labels close to gold labels and far above no demonstrations. Examples supply label space, input distribution and format.
quote: ground truth demonstrations are in fact not required
limits: Classification and multi-choice only, not multi-step reasoning. Differs from human data where correct examples did better (Barbieri).
agent_relevance: A split between people and models: for models, format and distribution of cases may matter more than correctness on simple tasks.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-shot in-context learning: MATH
finding: More solved examples help up to a point; for ground-truth human solutions on MATH500 the score peaks near 125 examples and then declines.
numbers: MATH500, 5 seeds. Reinforced ICL (model-written solutions) plateaus around 25 examples, about 5% above human-solution ICL, and does not drop at very large counts. Unsupervised ICL (problems only) comparable or better than problems with solutions. 4-shot Minerva baseline: 55.7% MATH500, 90.6% GSM8K.
quote: solutions may be redundant for eliciting problem-solving via in-context learning
limits: Strong pretraining on math likely makes solutions redundant. Single model family (Gemini 1.5 Pro).
agent_relevance: Matches an expertise-reversal pattern for models: for domains the model knows, solutions add little. Keep the example set small and model-written ones are fine.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-shot ICL: GPQA
finding: On graduate-level GPQA, model-written rationales help consistently while problems alone only match or beat zero-shot.
numbers: GPQA diamond (198 problems) test; 250 non-diamond problems as shots. 125-shot prompts with human or model rationales beat 40.4% (Claude-3 Sonnet reported). Reinforced ICL consistently beat zero-shot; Unsupervised ICL matched or beat it.
limits: Small test set (198), so noisy. Not a randomised test of worked examples vs problem solving per se.
agent_relevance: Where the model lacks the skill, rationales (worked solutions) matter; where it already has it, they do not.

source: Shang et al. (2026) CoThinker: LLM coordination under cognitive load theory (TMLR)
finding: Frames long prompts with many demonstrations as load on a bounded attention budget; cites Agarwal's drop with more examples as a redundancy-type effect.
numbers: Appendix B.1.4 reading of prior work: performance can fall with more in-context examples on hard tasks such as MATH, and scores can fall while NLL improves. Main result: gains concentrate on reasoning-heavy tasks; coordination overhead dominates on low-load tasks. Numbers not extracted from main tables.
limits: The CLT link is an analogy by the authors, not a test. I read the appendix framing, not the result tables.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a CLT-for-LLM analogy as evidence. Test example count on our own tasks.

source: Barbieri et al. (2023) poster: discrepancy with final paper
finding: The interim and final analyses disagree on moderators (none significant vs self-explanation significant), a sign the moderator findings are fragile.
numbers: Poster g = 0.43 (185 effect sizes); published g = 0.48 (43 studies per secondary source).
limits: Differences in study sets are not documented in what I read.
agent_relevance: Weight the average effect more than any single moderator claim.

source: IES practice guide (2007) as cited in Barbieri poster
finding: IES guide gave moderate evidence for interleaving worked examples with problem solving in math.
numbers: Only 5 of the 40 articles in the meta-analysis were published by 2007, so most evidence is newer than the guide.
limits: Guide itself not opened.
agent_relevance: Interleaving solved cases with attempts is the evidence-backed pattern, not examples alone.

source: Quilici and Mayer (1996) and Paas (1992), as listed in Wikipedia: null results
finding: Reported null or equivalent results: more examples per type did not improve problem sorting; completion problems equalled full examples.
numbers: No numbers available in the source opened.
limits: Original papers not opened; unverified from Wikipedia only.
agent_relevance: Marks where more examples gives no gain.

source: Rourke and Sweller (2009) via Sweller (2011): design history
finding: Worked example effect shown outside math: novices learning to recognise furniture designers' styles.
numbers: No numbers in the source opened.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Hints that cases may help in less formal tasks.

source: Task-type limit: Nievelstein et al. (2013) law case reasoning, via Wikipedia
finding: Less structured legal reasoning still showed an efficiency benefit for examples, for both novice and advanced students.
numbers: No numbers available.
limits: Original not opened. Advanced students were not harmed here, unlike expertise reversal findings elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Efficiency gain may survive in open tasks, but check.

source: Hou et al. (2026) related work on adaptive fading in tutors
finding: Related-work section notes pre-LLM tutors adjust help up and down: adaptive fading brings a worked step back when mastery falls.
numbers: Cites QUADRATIC (hint level down after correct move, up on request), Ecolab (five help levels). One LLM tutor moves both ways within a conversation.
limits: Literature survey inside an HCI paper; claims not checked.
agent_relevance: Design precedent for a fade-and-return rule driven by checks.

source: Wang et al. (2023) error analysis of invalid-reasoning demonstrations
finding: Calculation and semantic-understanding errors dominate when invalid demonstrations produce wrong answers.
numbers: Error table: where CoT is correct but invalid-reasoning prompt is wrong, 35% semantic understanding, 20% one step missing; where CoT wrong but invalid right, 25% semantic. Small hand-labelled sample.
limits: Sample size small and unclear in text read.
agent_relevance: Limited evidence; use only as hint.
